oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hoshana Rabbah, Dovid HaMelech's day, is the day of the aravah, the lowest of the four kinds, whose power belongs to the fallen souls of the last generation and defeats the heavenly war of Gog uMagog.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Hoshana Rabbah as the seventh day of Sukkos, the day of Dovid HaMelech, who descends to the lowest souls, the souls of the aravah. He explains that the aravah outside the Beis HaMikdash is, according to the Rambam, only a custom of the prophets, yet the calendar was fixed so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos, even though Rosh Hashanah and the first day of Sukkos may, setting aside shofar and lulav. He answers that the four kinds are four levels of Jews and of generations, and ours is the aravah; the Chachamim arranged the aravah for these fallen souls. It must be on a weekday, when the nations, fattened by the seventy bulls, wage the war of Gog uMagog in heaven, and the beaten aravah defeats them. Dovid gathers the broken and indebted around him; Hashem does not despise the prayer of the last generation, and the Mashgiach calls everyone to help rebuild the fallen sukkah of Dovid.

en: Hoshana Rabbah is Dovid HaMelech's day, and Dovid, the middah of malchus, lowers himself to the lowest souls, the souls of the aravah.
Although the aravah today is only a custom of the prophets, the calendar was fixed so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos, even at the cost of shofar and lulav on Shabbos.
The four kinds are four levels of Jews and of generations; the generation before Moshiach, ours, is the aravah, the fallen souls.
Shabbos itself can stand in for shofar and lulav, but the aravah is needed on a weekday, when the forces of evil come out in strength.
Every Hoshana Rabbah there is a war of Gog uMagog in heaven, and the aravah, the lowest generations, is what defeats it.
Hashem does not despise the prayer of the last, fallen generation, and through its tefillos the fallen sukkah of Dovid will be rebuilt.

The Chachamim, foreseeing these fallen souls, protected the aravah from Shabbos, because Shabbos can replace shofar and lulav but the aravah is needed on a weekday, when it fights the war of Gog uMagog.

title.en: The heavenly war of Gog uMagog

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the nations, fattened by the seventy bulls of Sukkos, gathering strength on Hoshana Rabbah to wage war in heaven against Hashem and His Moshiach. He explains that the beaten aravah, the lowest generation, defeats Gog uMagog, whose gematria is seventy, and breaks the barrier between Klal Yisrael and the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Dovid gathers the broken souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Dovid HaMelech, the last middah of malchus, is the leader of the fallen souls, the fallen sukkah of Dovid. He reads the passuk that every man in distress, in debt and bitter of soul gathered to Dovid, applies it to Jews who feel they have done nothing for Hashem, and says the aravah's prayer is the prayer Hashem turns to.

title.en: Rebuilding the fallen sukkah of Dovid

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the passuk about the last generation teaches that the prayers of the fallen aravah generation are not despised, and that the sukkah of Dovid will be rebuilt. He calls everyone to gather around Dovid, to sing his zemiros and help rebuild the sukkah with tefillah, lulav and hakafos, and closes with blessings for a good kvittel and the redemption.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Akeidah was Avraham Avinu's hardest test because he saw Hashem only 'from a distance', confused by questions he could not answer, and that Klal Yisrael at the end of the golus is living through that same tenth test.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas HaAkeidah, said every morning, and asks why the last of Avraham's ten tests was the hardest. He contrasts it with the first test, Ur Kasdim, where Avraham, searching for the truth, gave his life for a Creator he had never seen. A test, he explains from the double meaning of nisayon, is meant to raise a person, so each one is harder than the last. The Zohar points to 'he saw the place from a distance': at the Akeidah Avraham felt far from Hashem, because the command contradicted the promise that his seed would come from Yitzchak, and kashyos about Hashem's truth entered his mind. He pushed them away and went blindly. Why he did not notice that he was only told to bring Yitzchak up, as Rashi explains, is answered: when Hashem does not want a person to know, he does not know, as with Haman and the seventh of Adar. Following the Ramban that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's, the Mashgiach says Klal Yisrael now faces the tenth test of hester panim and must hold on to emunah.

en: The Akeidah, the tenth and last of Avraham's tests, was the hardest; had he failed it, the Mashgiach says, all the earlier tests would have been lost.
A nisayon is also a raising, like a flag (nes) held high: every test is meant to promote a person, so each test is harder than the one before.
At the Akeidah Avraham saw Hashem 'from a distance': the command to slaughter Yitzchak seemed to contradict the promise that his seed would come through Yitzchak, and kashyos made him feel estranged.
Avraham dismissed the kashyos, covered his eyes, said Shema Yisrael and went to the Akeidah blindly, without giving the questions any place in his mind.
When Hashem does not want a person to know something, even the wisest cannot figure it out; so it was with Avraham at the Akeidah and with Haman and the seventh of Adar.

Following the Ramban that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's, Klal Yisrael at the end of the golus is going through Avraham's tenth test of hester panim, and those who hold on to emunah will pass it.

title.en: The Akeidah: the hardest of the ten tests

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas HaAkeidah, said every morning, and asks why it is the climax of tefillah. He asks who in the room would not obey if Hashem appeared and commanded him, and notes that Avraham passed all ten tests, the Akeidah being the last and hardest.

title.en: The first test: Ur Kasdim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how young Avraham searched for the truth, rejected the sun and the moon, concluded there is one Creator, defied Nimrod and was thrown into the fire unharmed. Hashem then revealed Himself to him, but in Ur Kasdim Avraham gave his life for a G-d he had never seen.

title.en: Nisayon means raising; seeing Hashem from afar

summary.en: From lashon hakodesh, where nisayon also means raising, the Mashgiach explains that every test is meant to promote, so each is harder than the last. He then asks why the Akeidah was harder than Ur Kasdim and brings the Zohar's hint: 'he saw the Place from a distance', echoed in the haftarah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Avraham's confusion and his blind faith

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Avraham's inner turmoil: Hashem is Emes and keeps His word, yet the command to slaughter Yitzchak contradicted the promise of seed through him. Avraham pushed the kashyos away, covered his eyes and said Shema, and went blindly; afterwards he asked the malach why Hashem had changed His mind, and was told, as Rashi brings, that he was only told to bring Yitzchak up.

title.en: When Hashem hides, one does not know

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Avraham, who understood Hashem more than the malachim, missed what a child learning Rashi sees, and answers that when Hashem tests a person and does not want him to know, he does not know. He applies the same answer to Haman, who calculated that Moshe died on the seventh of Adar but did not realize he was also born then.

title.en: Maaseh avos siman labanim: the tenth test today

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the Akeidah a test of hester panim and brings the Ramban in Lech Lecha that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's: the famine, Pharaoh taking Sarah, the plagues and the gifts. By that pattern Klal Yisrael goes through Avraham's ten tests, and at the end of the golus faces the tenth: a whole world full of kashyos, from the Holocaust to the darkness of most of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Holding on to emunah until Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls books written after the war questioning Hashem, and says that today a handful of Yidden who believe are living through Avraham's last test, with the promise that emunah will prevail. Like Avraham, one must cover one's eyes and say Shema and 'Hashem Elokeichem Emes'; the added word Emes corresponds to the 'eikev', the heels of Moshiach, which is why Avraham was told 'eikev asher shamata bekoli'.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach gathers teachings from the sefarim hakedoshim on Elul as a month of Hashem's love and of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, when the way to teshuvah is open even to one sunk in sin, and he warns that not using it is worse than the sin itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Elul as a month of love, 'Ani ledodi vedodi li', and of great success, and urges not to leave teshuvah for Rosh Hashanah. He brings the Arizal that Elul is governed by 'Who makes a way in the sea', a way back even for one drowned in sin, and the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy that no sin can reach. With the king in the field and a story of Rebbe Elimelech, he shows how near Hashem is and how the shofar of Elul terrifies the forces of impurity. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the forty days are a mikveh, explains how tzaddikim join one who does their mitzvah, and cites the daily bas kol. With the Midrash of the escaped prisoners he warns that wasting Elul is worse than the sin, and closes with emulating Hashem's middos and davening for the geulah.

en: Elul is a month of love from Heaven and of great success and siyata dishmaya, and teshuvah belongs in Elul, not left for Rosh Hashanah.
According to the Arizal Elul is governed by the passuk 'Who makes a way in the sea': even one sunk in a sea of sins is given a way back.
Elul is the time of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, which do not depend on a person's deeds and which no sin or blemish can reach.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are a mikveh, completed at the close of Yom Kippur.
One who does a mitzvah that a tzaddik was devoted to draws that tzaddik's soul to join him, and in Elul the tzaddikim of the generation of the desert help a person do teshuvah.
Not using the month Hashem gives for teshuvah is worse than the sin itself.
One merits the Thirteen Attributes by emulating Hashem's middos toward other Jews, which is why the Yismach Yisrael says to learn Tomer Devorah in Elul.

title.en: Elul, a month of love and success

He urges preparing in Elul with purity so as to enter Rosh Hashanah with joy, and not leaving teshuvah for Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: A way in the sea and the Thirteen Attributes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that Elul is governed by 'Who makes a way in the sea', with a chassid's teaching that the 'sea' is teshuvah, and explains that even one drowned in sins is given a way. Elul is the time of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, its forty days hinted in the four yuds of 'Ani ledodi vedodi li', when the second luchos were given for sinners; he ends with the mashal of the king in the field.

title.en: Rebbe Elimelech's letter and the shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story of a woman whose husband was seized by the forces of impurity; Rebbe Elimelech sent her with a letter to a house in the forest, and they released him. The man remembered only that when Jews blew the shofar on Rosh Chodesh Elul, his captors were seized with terrible fear.

title.en: The forty days as a mikveh

summary.en: The Mashgiach touches on the dispute over Nissan and Tishrei, Tishrei being judgment and Nissan mercy. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the forty days hold as many hours as a mikveh holds lugin, explains how tzaddikim make such a mikveh whole again, and that it is completed at the end of Yom Kippur, with the closing mishnah of Yoma, 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem'.

title.en: When tzaddikim join a person's mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Chaim Vital's account that the Arizal stood up when he entered, because Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair came in with him. From this he explains that a tzaddik's soul joins one who does his mitzvah: Avraham with visiting the sick and Shacharis, the Avos with the three tefillos and Shabbos meals, and in Elul the tzaddikim of the desert generation with teshuvah.

title.en: The days of Elul cry out

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the daily bas kol, 'Return, wayward children', and the Ba'al Shem Tov that a pure heart hears it; in Elul the days themselves cry out, so even the deaf can hear. He then brings Rabbeinu Yonah's Midrash of prisoners who fled through a tunnel the king dug, while one stayed behind, to show that not doing teshuvah in Elul is worse than the sin.

title.en: Emulating the middos, and a closing tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yismach Yisrael, citing Likkutei Torah, that 'Ani ledodi vedodi li' is the Thirteen Attributes, merited by emulating Hashem's mercy and kindness toward other Jews, which is why one should learn Tomer Devorah in Elul. He describes the Thirteen Attributes as a holy of holies no accuser enters, and closes by urging Jews to use Elul and daven for themselves and all of Klal Yisrael for a year of geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that because Purim stems from the fiftieth level that is above time, Adar Sheni only repeats Adar Rishon, so the Purim of Adar Sheni is already present on Purim Katan, and the joy Jews add on their own is the acceptance of the Torah with love.

abstract.en: After a niggun, the Mashgiach raises a question on the Bnei Yissaschar: Tu B'Shvat is forty days before 25 Adar, when creation began, but in a leap year it is sixty days. He brings the Maharal that the Purim miracle is above time, from the fiftieth level, and uses this to answer the Magen Avraham's question on calling Shavuos the time of the giving of the Torah when it was given on the fifty-first day. Like a page of Gemara reviewed the next day, Adar Sheni only repeats Adar Rishon. He then brings the Chasam Sofer that a miracle obligates a day of thanks from the Torah, and that zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur. This is why Purim Katan forbids eulogies and fasting. He asks how a prohibition fulfils the remembrance and answers that the Purim of Adar Sheni is already present, and that the joy the Chachamim left to the Jews themselves is the acceptance of the Torah with love.

en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal that the miracle of Purim comes from the fiftieth level, which is above time.
Because Adar comes from the fiftieth day, Adar Sheni is a review of Adar Rishon, so the calendar's sixty days hold only thirty days of Adar.
According to the Chasam Sofer, a miracle obligates a Jew from the Torah to make a day of thanks to Hashem, and zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur mitzvah.
The Mashgiach explains that the prohibition of eulogies and fasting on Purim Katan is how the Torah obligation of remembering the miracle is fulfilled in Adar Rishon.
Purim is an acceptance of the Torah with love, and the Chachamim left the festive joy to the Jews themselves so that they would do it of their own accord.

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the Bnei Yissaschar's forty days from Tu B'Shvat to 25 Adar works in a leap year, when it is sixty days. He then brings the Maharal that the Purim miracle is above time, coming from the fiftieth level, and shows the haste of the Megillah's events.

title.en: The fiftieth day and the two Adars

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the Magen Avraham's question on 'the time of the giving of our Torah': the fiftieth day is above time and includes the fifty-first. With a mashal of a page of Gemara reviewed the next day, he explains that Adar Sheni repeats Adar Rishon, which answers the Bnei Yissaschar question, and that today is in truth also Purim.

title.en: Chasam Sofer: a miracle obligates thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that a miracle obligates a Jew from the Torah to make a day of thanks, learned from the Gemara's kal vachomer from the shirah at the Yam Suf, and that the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah set its details. He adds the Chasam Sofer's and Chacham Tzvi's ruling that zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur.

title.en: Why Purim Katan forbids eulogy and fasting

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because zrizin makdimin applies, Adar Rishon must already carry a remembrance of the miracle, which is the prohibition of eulogy and fasting; the other details move to Adar Sheni for semichas geulah l'geulah, using the Chasam Sofer's distinction from ein maavirin al hamitzvos. He then asks how a mere prohibition can be a fulfilment.

title.en: Purim Katan and accepting the Torah with love

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the Purim of Adar Sheni is already present on Purim Katan, and that Purim's essence is the acceptance of the Torah with love. The Chachamim did not make the festive gathering a mitzvah, leaving it to the Jews to rejoice on their own, and this joy on Purim Katan is that acceptance with love.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai, while busy saving lives, saw the inner Torah within the events of the Megillah, so that only those Sanhedrin members whose portion was the plain level of Torah saw his work as a loss of Torah study.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach starts from the Gemara that Mordechai was first counted fourth among the leaders who went up to Eretz Yisroel and later fifth, from which Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives, and asks how this fits with Mordechai's greatness. He brings the Gemara that Rabbi Meir wrote a Megillah from memory and explains, with the Midrash that Rabbi Meir's Torah read 'garments of light', that Rabbi Meir saw through the outer skin of creation to the Torah inside it, so he copied the Megillah from creation itself. He then brings the eight kings of Edom, where Divrei Hayamim, written by Ezra, says the eighth king died while the Torah does not, and distinguishes, through the Gemara about Moshe and Rabbi Akiva, between seeing with prophecy and understanding with wisdom. From his level of prophecy Ezra did not see Mordechai's inner Torah. So too some of the Sanhedrin, whose portion was the plain meaning, as in the stories of the Beis Yosef and of a student of the Lechovitcher. The majority saw Mordechai's greatness.

en: From Mordechai being counted fourth and later fifth, Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives.
The world was created through the Torah, so every part of creation is a part of the Torah, and a higher person sees that inner Torah rather than the outer shell.
Rabbi Meir could look through the 'skin' covering creation and see the Torah in it, which is how he could write a Megillah without a written copy.
A prophet sees with his eyes, while a sage understands with wisdom; one can grasp a matter with wisdom without having reached it in prophecy.
While Mordechai worked to save lives he saw the inner Torah of the Megillah's events, so for him it was no loss of Torah study.
Some of the Sanhedrin, whose portion in Torah was its plain meaning, saw it as a loss of Torah study and separated from him, while the majority saw his greatness.

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Arizal told the Beis Yosef that his portion is in halacha, and how the Lechovitcher told a great student not to learn kabbalah because his portion is the plain meaning. So too the minority of the Sanhedrin saw Mordechai's work as a loss of Torah, while the majority saw his greatness; he ends with Mordechai's greatness.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Satan, sensing his end as Moshiach approaches, fights emunah with all his strength, and that after failing to 'bite' the Jews through persecution, Esav now 'bites with a kiss' through friendliness, assimilation and the invasion of the Jewish home.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that every person and every generation has a mitzvah of its own, and that in the generation before Moshiach that mitzvah is emunah, as Chavakuk established all the mitzvos on emunah. Because the Satan opposes whatever mitzvah is a person's success, the world today is a battlefield against emunah, just as in Mitzrayim the Jews first believed Moshe and then lost faith when the slavery grew harder. A being in mortal danger fights with new strength, like a dying candle that flares up; the Satan, who will be removed when Moshiach comes, is gasping for life. The Tosfos Yom Tov explains that it was a miracle the Kohen Gadol stayed tahor because the Satan concentrated on him alone. The Sfas Emes explains that Esav, unable to bite Yaakov, 'bit him with a kiss'. The Mashgiach applies this to the Church's new friendliness, to assimilation, and to the Satan's 'last wish': entering the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television.

en: Every generation has a mitzvah of its own, and in the generation before the Geulah it is emunah.
The Satan opposes whatever mitzvah is a person's main success, so today the whole world is a battlefield against emunah.
Because the Satan will be removed when Moshiach comes, he fights now with the desperate strength of a dying being, like a candle that flares up before it goes out.
Esav, unable to destroy the Jews by persecution, now 'bites with a kiss' through friendliness and assimilation, which does more damage than the persecution did.
The Satan has been granted a 'last wish' to pass the mezuzah, and he now enters the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one in danger discovers new strength, and that the Satan, who will be removed when Moshiach comes, therefore fights emunah with all his might. He compares this to a person's last struggle and to a candle that shoots up high flames before it goes out.

title.en: The Kohen Gadol's miracle and our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah in Avos that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur, and the Tosfos Yom Tov's question how that is a miracle given all the precautions; the answer is that the Satan concentrated all his force on him. So too, since all signs show that this generation may see Moshiach, the Satan concentrates on it, and that is why emunah is so hard to keep today.

title.en: Vayishakehu: Esav bites with a kiss

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi and the Midrash on 'vayishakehu', that Esav wanted to bite Yaakov and kissed him instead, and the Sfas Emes's question and answer: unable to bite with a bite, he bit with a kiss. He applies it to the Church, which persecuted the Jews through the galus and now harms them far more with friendliness, assimilation and intermarriage.

title.en: The Satan's last wish: the invaded home

summary.en: The Mashgiach points to the Pope's recent apology and visit to the Kosel as the kiss that bites, and says most Jews have fallen to it. Bringing the Gemara that the kingdom on earth resembles the kingdom of heaven, he compares the Satan to a condemned man granted a last wish: he may now pass the mezuzah and enter the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television. He closes that one must guard what one reads and sees and will discuss next week how to keep emunah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that although the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, on Purim Katan it is read in Heaven in the yeshivah of Rabbi Yosi, and its lights come down to break the concealment of Adar Rishon.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah's wording 'megillah nikreis', the Megillah 'is read', and notes that every word hints at many matters. He brings the passuk of the two great luminaries: the moon, the smaller light, is Knesses Yisrael, diminished both in its light and in its year, which is about ten days shorter than the sun's. Each year the moon falls further behind, until in Adar Sheni of the leap year the two are evened out, so Adar Rishon is the time of distance. The halachah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, but Rabbi Yosi holds Adar Rishon, and both are the words of the living G-d. In Rabbi Yosi's heavenly yeshivah the Megillah is read on Purim Katan, and its lights break the concealment. The Mashgiach closes with Purim as a new Matan Torah, unity, and brachos.

en: The moon, the smaller luminary, represents Knesses Yisrael, and it was diminished both in its light and in the length of its year.
Each year the moon falls further behind the sun, until the leap year, when in Adar Sheni the sun's year and the moon's year are evened out; Adar Rishon is the time of distance.

Although the halachah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, Rabbi Yosi's view that it is read in Adar Rishon is also true, since both are the words of the living G-d.
On Purim Katan the Megillah is read in Heaven, in Rabbi Yosi's yeshivah, and great lights come down that break the concealment of Adar Rishon.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Esther's words that she had not been called before the king for thirty days, noting that thirty days marks a new period. Citing the Rambam, he explains that one who davens must know he stands before the King, that each word of tefillah is a heichal, and that before every aliyah comes a yeridah. In his first approach, Esther, about to rise to 'vatilbash Esther malchus', felt for thirty days that she could not say a warm word before Hashem; Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech', and the Mashgiach compares Avraham sitting at the opening of the tent, who then received the revelation. en: Thirty days is a set period of time; after thirty days a new period begins, which is why Esther counted thirty days without being called.
One who davens must know that he stands before the King; each word of tefillah is a heichal, and one goes from one heichal to the next.

Esther felt for thirty days that she could not say a warm word before Hashem and asked how she could bring a yeshuah; Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech', not to make calculations about herself.
A descent comes before an ascent and is its preparation, as with Avraham Avinu, who sat at the opening of the tent and precisely then received a great revelation.

In a second approach, the thirty days were the thirty days before Pesach, in which Esther was preparing herself in purity, and Mordechai told her that her personal preparation must yield to the need of Klal Yisroel.
The Mashgiach applies this to the present: looking at the time, one must prepare for a great yeshuah and daven for the klal, not only for oneself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the first of the Ten Commandments, which ties emunah to Yetzias Mitzrayim, and explains that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah. At Yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem showed that He created the world: the ten utterances of creation, which no one saw, were revealed in the ten plagues, and the last plague, of the firstborn, matches the first utterance, Bereishis. Hashem therefore wants the story told to the children and also eaten, through matzah. The Mashgiach shows by gematria that bread holds the Divine Name three times, and matzah the Name with its filling three times. Matzah, baked fast, is above time and place, while chametz is bound to them; it is the food of emunah. Pesach and milah alone carry kareis because they bind a Jew to Avraham, his root. Nisan, the spring, is a new beginning and the month of chesed, and the Mashgiach calls on each person to renew himself with it.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and therefore it is the Yom Tov of emunah.
At Yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem revealed, through the ten plagues, the ten utterances with which He created the world.
Hashem wants Yetzias Mitzrayim not only told to the children but eaten, so that through the matzah it becomes part of a person.
Matzah is above time and place, while chametz is bound to them, so matzah is the food of emunah.
Pesach and milah are the only positive mitzvos that carry kareis, because both bind a Jew to Avraham Avinu, his root.
Nisan, the spring, is a new beginning and the month of chesed, and a person must renew himself together with all of creation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Arizal's words that it is a mitzvah to rejoice in the simcha of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who asked that people rejoice on his hillula. Rashbi was not grasped even by his colleagues, which is why the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda; in the future, when the world is filled with knowledge of Hashem, it will follow Rabbi Shimon. Yet even the lowest Jew has a place at his simcha. The Mashgiach then tells of Rashbi's miracles, above all the valley he filled with golden dinars, and asks why the Midrash calls the taking back of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's gift a greater miracle but says nothing of the kind about Rashbi. He answers that the gold was Rashbi's own Torah secrets spread over Meron, which took material form because the students showed interest in wealth; it was no gift from heaven, and when they held back it returned to Torah. He closes with blessings that Rashbi's merit bring the redemption, and with the niggun the Satmar Rav learned in Meron.

en: Following the Arizal and the Zohar, the Mashgiach says it is a mitzvah and a nachas for every Jew to rejoice on the hillula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.
The halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda rather than Rabbi Shimon because his contemporaries could not grasp him; in the future, when the world is full of knowledge of Hashem, it will follow Rabbi Shimon.
The golden dinars that filled the valley of Meron were Rashbi's chiddushei Torah, which took material form because his students showed interest in wealth.
Since the gold was not sent from heaven but was Torah already present in Meron, its disappearance was no miracle: it simply returned to being Torah.
Rashbi said he could free the whole world from judgment, and the Mashgiach prays that his merit bring the redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by tying the nights of Chanukah to the middos and says Chanukah is the yom tov of hod. He brings the Lubavitcher Rebbe's observation that on the fifth night Beis Hillel's count first exceeds Beis Shammai's, and the Ramban that the Chanukah lights of Aharon's descendants are Aharon's lasting share. Hod means both admitting and praising, and the two are one: only someone who feels nothing is owed him can truly thank, as Aharon rejoiced when Moshe was chosen. The Jewish day, davening and Shabbos all open with thanks; Yehudah, named for thanks, and Matisyahu, a spark of Yehudah, set Chanukah for praise. In the future only the korban todah remains, so one must learn here to delight in praise, above all on Shabbos and through song. He tells of a camp survivor saved by stolen bread, speaks of the hundred berachos, and reads a tzaddik's will thanking Hashem for every small thing.

en: Chanukah is the yom tov of the middah of hod, and the fifth night, the night of hod, was especially cherished by tzaddikim.
Hod means both admitting and praising, and both come from shiflus: only one who feels nothing is owed to him can thank with his whole heart.
The Jewish day begins with Modeh Ani, davening begins with Hodu and Mizmor l'Todah, and Shabbos begins with Tov l'hodos: thanks is the beginning that includes everything.
In the future only the korban todah will remain, so a person must accustom himself here, above all on Shabbos, to delight in praising Hashem.
Each yom tov's middah is meant for the whole year, and from Chanukah one draws hod: thanking Hashem for every small thing, even for what is not good.
Thanking Hashem for every detail rests on emunah in hashgacha pratis, and the Mashgiach says anyone can get used to it without being a great baal madreigah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that in the low generation before Moshiach, those raised in Torah homes carry the responsibility of passing emunah on. Our faith rests on what millions of Jews saw from Yetzias Mitzrayim to Matan Torah, written in the Torah while they were alive and handed down unchanged. Small differences between communities reflect the twelve shevatim, each with its own color, gate and path, while the Torah and Chazal's decrees bind everyone; disputes such as an eruv belong to the rabbanim, and the Chasam Sofer warns that machlokes can delay Moshiach. Pesach, the yom tov of emunah, exists to pass this down, which is why it carries kareis. Habakkuk based everything on emunah, so one must learn it, not treat it as a habit. A story of neshamos protesting endless gilgulim ends with Hashem asking only for emunah without 'would have'. The Mashgiach illustrates hashgachah pratis and calls Pesach a time to strengthen emunah.

en: Jewish emunah rests on a mesorah no other faith has: millions saw Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, it was written down while they were alive, and the same Sefer Torah is found wherever Jews are.
Differences in minhagim and small details between communities stem from the twelve shevatim, each with its own color, gate and path, while all of Klal Yisrael shares the Torah and Chazal's decrees.
Pesach exists to pass emunah from generation to generation, which is why it alone among the yomim tovim carries kareis.
Emunah must be learned and researched, not lived as an inherited habit, since it is the Jew's very neshamah for which whole communities gave their lives.
Complete emunah means believing that every detail is directed by Hashem, so a person never says 'would have, could have, should have'.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that small differences in Sifrei Torah and minhagim come from the twelve shevatim, each with its own gate in heaven, stone on the choshen and flag color. He brings Rashi on the flags, a reading of 'shoftim v'shotrim' with 'lishvatecha', the gates at the end of Yechezkel, the Zohar on twelve gates for tefillah, and the twelve paths at Kriyas Yam Suf.

title.en: Machlokes, the Chasam Sofer, and what binds all

summary.en: Applying this to a dispute over an eruv, the Mashgiach cites the Chazon Ish that each person follows his rav, and the Chasam Sofer that machlokes in the generation of great Acharonim held back Moshiach. He stresses that differences are only in small details, while the Torah and Chazal's decrees bind every Jew, and this unbroken mesorah is our strength against apikorsim.

title.en: Pesach, the yom tov of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah of emunah is 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha asher hotzeisicha', since the ten makkos revealed the ten maamaros of creation, and that Pesach is the yom tov for passing emunah to the children, which is why it carries kareis. Before Moshiach the yetzer hara fights hardest, so, as the Gemara says Habakkuk based all on emunah, one must learn and research emunah rather than treat it as a tradition.

title.en: The neshamos who protested their gilgulim

summary.en: After describing communities that gave their lives rather than give up emunah, the Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who, after Kiddush Levanah, told his talmidim what he had seen: neshamos tired of being sent down again and again went from malach to malach up to Hashem, asking what He wants of them. Hashem answers that they should go down and have emunah.

title.en: Hashgachah pratis: no 'would have'

summary.en: Hashem's condition is emunah so complete that a person never says 'would have', illustrated by a man who blames his wife for a missed train and a lost deal. The Mashgiach describes hashgachah pratis down to a falling straw and the kernels in a loaf of bread, Hashem as the One who cares for a person more than anyone, and closes that Pesach is a time for introspection and fortifying emunah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach reads the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream standing in astonishment beside the fat ones as the sitra achra, and Hashem Himself, marveling at the Jewish soul's mesiras nefesh, seen at Chanukah, in the Alter Rebbe and the Rebbes of Lubavitch, and in the shluchim of today.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream first stood beside the fat ones before swallowing them, and why Pharaoh left this out when he retold the dream. With Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch's reading of 'our feet stood in your gates, Yerushalayim' he explains standing as being frozen in wonder. The fat cows are the G-dly soul with its seven holy middos, the lean ones the animal soul; even when the holy soul seems swallowed, the sitra achra stands amazed before it, and Hashem Himself marvels, as the Gemara brings from Zechariah. Pharaoh, ashamed, hid this. At Chanukah the Jews felt the loss of Torah as a true tzarah and gave their lives, and so the Rambam calls the mitzvah very dear, like Avraham's milah that came through pain. The Mashgiach ends with the mesiras nefesh of the Alter Rebbe, the Lubavitcher Rebbes and the shluchim.

en: The fat cows are the G-dly soul with its seven holy middos, and the lean cows are the animal soul with its seven middos, which can swallow the holy soul into exile.
The lean cows' standing is the sitra achra stopping in astonishment before the greatness of a Jewish soul, which it cannot truly swallow.
Hashem Himself marvels at how Jews withstood the exile, as the Gemara brings from the passuk in Zechariah 'it will also be wondrous in My eyes'.
Pharaoh left the standing out of his retelling out of shame, and his claim that the swallowed cows could not be recognized is a lie: the Jewish soul remains and acts.

At Chanukah the Jews felt the loss of Torah and mitzvos as a real tzarah and gave their lives for it; therefore the Rambam calls Chanukah a very dear mitzvah, as a mitzvah that comes through pain is dear.
The Alter Rebbe and all the Rebbes of Lubavitch gave their lives for Chassidus, and the last Rebbe's shluchim continue that mesiras nefesh, at which the world and Hashem marvel.

title.en: Why the lean cows stood still

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the starving cows in Pharaoh's dream stood beside the fat ones instead of swallowing them at once, and why Pharaoh omitted this when retelling the dream. He brings Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch's explanation that 'our feet stood in your gates, Yerushalayim' means being frozen in awe.

title.en: The animal soul stands amazed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the fat cows as the G-dly soul and the lean ones as the animal soul, and says that the sitra achra, and Hashem Himself as the Gemara brings from Zechariah, marvel at the Jewish soul surviving in exile. Pharaoh hid this out of shame and falsely claimed the swallowed cows left no trace.

title.en: Chanukah: a tzarah only Jews feel

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Greeks' decrees against Torah: a gentile wonders what kind of tzarah that is, but for Jews it was a true tzarah, and they gave their lives, so Hashem marveled and brought the salvation and the Chanukah lights. He explains the Rambam's 'very dear mitzvah' through Rashi on Avraham's oath by the milah, which came through pain.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh of Lubavitch and the shluchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Alter Rebbe and all the Lubavitcher Rebbes giving their lives for Chassidus, the Rayatz demanding mesiras nefesh of his chassidim, and the last Rebbe's shluchim, four thousand of whom were recently photographed at 770. The world and Hashem marvel, and he closes with a wish for the Geulah, when the world will marvel at how Jews endured the exile.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the light of Shabbos, which lifts souls upward, with the light of Chanukah, which descends to the lowest places, and sees in this the path of the Chabad Rebbes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the pairs Hashem set in the world, holiness against its opposite, light against darkness, day against night, inside against outside, and notes that the Chanukah light belongs to night, darkness and the public domain. He brings the Midrash of Yaakov's ladder, where Yaakov saw the angels of the kingdoms rise and fall and Edom rise without end, and asks how the Midrash can say Yaakov did not believe. He contrasts the Shabbos light, which raises a Jew upward, with the Chanukah light, which can kindle even the 'disqualified oils'. Yaakov is the aspect of Shabbos, but some souls bound to him cannot hold on to it; for their sake Yaakov asked that the Shechinah come down below ten, and this became Chanukah. The Mashgiach applies this to the Alter Rebbe, who raised his chassidim, and to the later Chabad Rebbes, who went down to the lowest places.

en: The Chanukah light belongs to the side of night, darkness and the public domain, unlike the Menorah of the Beis HaMikdash.
Shabbos is the highest point in time and lifts a Jew upward, but some fallen souls cannot hold on to it.
What Shabbos cannot kindle, Chanukah can: the 'disqualified oils' not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah.
For the sake of the souls who cannot rise with him, Yaakov asked that the Shechinah come down to them, below ten, and from this came Chanukah.
The Alter Rebbe lifted his chassidim upward, like Shabbos, while the later Chabad Rebbes went down with the Chanukah light to the lowest places to raise Jews.

title.en: Chanukah's light and Yaakov's ladder

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the pairs of holiness and its opposite and shows that the Chanukah light belongs to night, darkness and the outside. He brings the Midrash of Yaakov's ladder and the angels of the kingdoms, and asks how the Midrash can say that Yaakov, the root of bitachon, did not believe.

title.en: The Shabbos light and the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Shabbos candle, inside and above ten, with the Chanukah candle, outside and below ten, and brings the Me'or Einayim that the oils not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah. He explains that Yaakov is the aspect of Shabbos, the trunk from which the twelve tribes branch out, and that some fallen souls cannot hold on to Shabbos to rise with it.

title.en: Yaakov's plea brings down the Shechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov saw the souls bound to him that had fallen to the side of Esav and could not believe, and that this is the meaning of the Midrash's 'he did not believe'. Yaakov refused to go up alone and asked that the Shechinah come down below ten; 'Hashem stood over him', and Hashem promised there would be a Chanukah.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe's Shabbos and Chabad's Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Alter Rebbe raised his chassidim to lofty levels, and tells of Reb Avraham Zuskin, whom he saw davening on Shabbos with tears for hours. He then says the later Chabad Rebbes did the opposite, going down with the Chanukah light through shluchim to Jews with no Jewish education, and closes with a tefillah that Jews spread chassidus and be redeemed.

oneLiner.en: On Zos Chanukah the Mashgiach teaches that the mizbe'ach and the Beis HaMikdash stand on unity among Jews, and that forgiving one another brings miracles and the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Zohar on Parshas Mikeitz: Rabbi Abba saw a man saved by two miracles, a snake killed beside him and a ledge that collapsed just after he left it. The man explained that he always forgave those who wronged him and even did them favors, and Rabbi Abba said his deeds were greater than Yosef's. The Mashgiach then turns to the reading of Zos Chanukah and asks why the Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings, which any child could add up. He answers that the mizbe'ach stands on achdus, as the Maharal says; the shared wagons broke down the walls between tribes, and the total shows twelve tribes became one. He brings the Midrash Tanchuma on unity, and the break between Yosef and his brothers that is healed in Vayigash, and prays for the last redemption through such unity. Finally he calls Zos Chanukah a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day when prayers are answered.

en: In the Zohar, a man who always forgave those who wronged him, and even did them good, merited miracle upon miracle; Rabbi Abba called his deeds greater than Yosef's.
The Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings to show that the mizbe'ach was inaugurated through the unity of all the tribes.
Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach says the Beis HaMikdash stands on achdus, and sinas chinam is why it was destroyed.
When Jews are united, the Midrash Tanchuma says, the attribute of judgment cannot touch them, even if they have sinned gravely.
The Mashgiach prays that, as the earlier exiles ended, the present exile end through Jews forgiving one another wholeheartedly, bringing a second chanukas hamizbe'ach.
Zos Chanukah is a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day of remembrance and salvation when prayers are accepted.

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells a Zohar on Mikeitz: a man sleeping on a mountain ledge near Lod was saved from a snake and from the ledge's collapse, and told Rabbi Abba that he always forgave those who wronged him and did them favors. He answers with the Maharal that the mizbe'ach stands on achdus: the shared wagons broke the walls between tribes and the total of a hundred and twenty is a new sum of one united people. He adds the Midrash Tanchuma that judgment cannot touch Jews when they are united.

title.en: Yosef's brothers and the prayer for unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yosef's brothers could not speak peaceably with him because they were men of truth, and shows the repair in Vayigash, where they spoke with him in love. He then prays that the present exile end as the earlier ones did, through Jews forgiving one another wholeheartedly, so that the 'second' chanukas hamizbe'ach, the building of the Beis HaMikdash, will come.

He then speaks of the treasures of Chanukah, citing the Skverer Rebbe, of Al HaNissim in bentching, and of the Rizhiner's prayer for mercy on the whole world.

catalogTitle: The Disintegration of Society at the Time of עקביתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the signs of the generation before Moshiach listed in the Gemara in Sotah are visible today, and explains that a Jew placed in this generation is meant to withstand its tests by keeping good company and holding on to emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the power of a person's company: the Rambam tells one to leave a bad neighborhood, the Chazon Ish told the Satmar Rav to run to the yeshiva, and a chassid was saved from sin only by shame before his friends. The Gemara's zarzir, a bird that keeps company with the raven, belongs to its kind. Today, he says, the outside world enters a Jew's own home, and souls are sent into this generation precisely to withstand these tests, as Yosef did in Mitzrayim. He then explains why the signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha appear on the 49th daf of Sotah, matching the 49 days of the Omer and the lowest level before redemption. Going through the Braisa, he shows its signs today: chutzpah, rising prices, a government turned to atheism, immoral universities, poverty of those from Eretz Yisrael, rebellious children and leaders who follow their congregations. Still, he concludes, one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

en: Company is the strongest influence on a person: what fear of Gehinnom and even a Rebbe cannot do, friends can do.
Unlike earlier generations, which lived apart from the nations, today the outside world enters the Jewish home through media and permissiveness.
Each soul is placed by Heaven into its generation for its tests and its tikkun; this generation was sent down to withstand these trials.
The signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha appear on daf 49 of Sotah, corresponding to the 49th, lowest day of the Omer count before the giving of the Torah.
The signs of the Braisa, such as chutzpah, rising prices, a government turned to atheism and rebellion of children, are visible in today's society.
Even in the last moments before redemption, one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

title.en: Why we were sent into this generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the separation Jews always had from the nations with today, when impurity enters the home through media and permissiveness. He explains that every soul is placed by Heaven into its generation for its tests and tikkun, as Yosef's trial in Mitzrayim had a purpose, and that this generation's task is to win these battles.

title.en: Sotah, the Omer and the 49th level

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sotah brings a barley offering, as does the Omer on the second day of Pesach, and that the 49 days of counting lead from the highest to the lowest level before the Torah is given. Since Masechta Sotah has 49 dapim, the Braisa of Ikvesa d'Meshicha on its 49th daf speaks of the last, lowest stage before the redemption.

title.en: Chutzpah and rising prices

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the Braisa's first signs: chutzpah at its peak, seen in the loss of respect for teachers, in protected subversive parades and in laws that permit wrongdoing, and prices rising even where supply is plentiful.

title.en: Government turned to atheism; schools of immorality

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that governments were always religious, even forcing their faith on Jews, while today the state is atheist; he tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov left a wagon whose driver did not cross himself. He then reads the 'house of meeting' as the institution of higher learning, now mixed and the source of immorality.

title.en: Poverty, rebellious children and failing leaders

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes people from Eretz Yisrael wandering abroad to collect money to marry off children, the young no longer standing for the old, children rebelling against parents, and leaders who, like a dog looking back at its master, follow their congregations. He concludes that even in these last moments one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

oneLiner.en: Through a piece of Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach explains that Chanukah opens the source of miracles, a level above nature, so that everything in these days comes through miracles, and he urges using the last day of Chanukah to draw on it.

abstract.en: After a word on the seudos of Chanukah, the Mashgiach turns to a piece of Sfas Emes. It asks why the blessing is 'she'asa nissim' if it refers to the miracle of the oil, and answers that the lighting is not chiefly for that miracle: Chanukah comes from a level above the seven days of nature, the source of miracles, which descends into time during these eight days. As during Sefirah everything relates to the day's sefirah, on Chanukah everything carries miracles; this is why even the first day, with enough oil, has a blessing. The Mashgiach applies this to the last day of Chanukah and to the present need of Jews for miracles, tells of Rabbi Shlomo Kluger and of Ruzhin on the worth of Chanukah, and closes with Chanukah as a time of pekidas akaros, also for one barren in Torah and tefillah.

en: Chanukah comes from a level above nature, the place from which miracles come, and that level descends into the world in these days.
Above the order of nature set in the seven days of creation there is an order of miracles, and on Chanukah it is joined to time.
The blessing 'she'asa nissim' is said not on the miracle of the oil but on the opening of the source of miracles in these days.
Everything on Chanukah, from the food to the candles, carries miracles, and even the first night's light burned from the source of miracles.
The Mashgiach says that on the last day of Chanukah one must work to connect to the source of miracles, since Jews today need miracles.
Chanukah is a time of pekidas akaros, and this includes one who is 'barren' in Torah or in tefillah.

title.en: Rabbi Shlomo Kluger, Ruzhin and the dreidel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a question put to Rabbi Shlomo Kluger by a prisoner let out for a short time, and of his answer favoring Hallel with the tzibbur over lighting. He cites the Ruzhiner that a simple Jew can accomplish on Chanukah what a tzaddik accomplishes with his tefillos, and tells of young men playing dreidel and the saying that what one wins on Chanukah cannot be lost.

title.en: Pekidas akaros and closing tefillah

summary.en: After a long niggun, the Mashgiach says Chanukah is a time of pekidas akaros like Rosh Hashanah, and, citing a Midrash, that barrenness includes one who sees no fruit in his Torah or tefillah. He urges using tomorrow's Hallel and Al Hanissim to ask that Jews be remembered with salvation and that barren Zion be remembered, with the ingathering of the exiles.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, corresponds to Shemini Atzeres and to the ushpiz of Shlomo HaMelech, the moon in its fullness, when holiness conquers the reshus harabim and turns it into a reshus hayachid, in the world and in each Jew's heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah standing beside Sukkos: Chanukah, like Sukkos, has eight days, so Zos Chanukah is the counterpart of Shemini Atzeres, whose ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech. The Chanukah light goes out into the reshus harabim, and holiness breaks into the place and the time of impurity, at the dark end of the month, in Teves. Shlomo, the fifteenth generation from Avraham, is the moon in its fullness; he took the daughters of kings to bring the nations under holiness and strove to bring the days of Moshiach, and even the two harlots, the chief feminine kelipos, submitted to him. Each Jew has his own reshus hayachid and reshus harabim, and Chanukah is the time to subdue the second to the first. After the churban, the festivals no longer gave enough strength for the whole year, so Hashem added Purim and then Chanukah as stations between Sukkos and Pesach. From Chanukah one takes thanksgiving for every small thing. He closes with the mashal of the queen who will return only if the king lifts her up, and a tefilah for Moshiach.

en: Since Chanukah has eight days like Sukkos, Zos Chanukah corresponds to Shemini Atzeres, whose ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech.
The Chanukah light enters the reshus harabim: holiness conquers both the place and the time that belonged to the other side and turns the public domain into a reshus hayachid.
Shlomo HaMelech is the moon in its fullness, and he took the daughters of kings in order to bring all the nations under holiness.
Every Jew has a reshus hayachid, the side of the heart that longs to serve Hashem, and a reshus harabim that wants only physical things; Chanukah is the time to subdue the second to the first.
After the churban the festivals no longer gave enough strength for the whole year, so Hashem gave Purim and later Chanukah as stations between Sukkos and Pesach.
What one takes from Chanukah is thanksgiving: thanking Hashem constantly, for every small thing.

He then explains that Shlomo, beloved of Hashem and author of Shir HaShirim, took the daughters of kings for the sake of Heaven, to bring the seventy nations under holiness.

title.en: Shlomo's striving for the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Pri Tzaddik that Shlomo tried to bring the days of Moshiach, when Hashem will be King over all the earth, and that in his days the sitra achra submitted to him. The two harlots who came before him were, as the Midrash says, the two chief feminine kelipos, and their submission came through his taking the daughters of kings; this is the power of Zos Chanukah.

title.en: The reshus harabim inside every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew is a small world, with a reshus hayachid in the right side of his heart and a reshus harabim in the left that wants only physical things. Chanukah, and Zos Chanukah above all, is the time to subdue one's reshus harabim so that even physical matters become for the sake of Heaven, as the kingdom of Yavan was handed over to the tzaddikim.

title.en: Purim and Chanukah as stations, and thanksgiving

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three festivals give strength for the whole year, but after the churban, without the Beis HaMikdash, it was not enough, so Hashem gave Purim and then, against the Greek culture of Yavan, Chanukah, as stations between Sukkos and Pesach. What one takes from Chanukah is thanking Hashem for every small thing, and he tells of an oved who thanked Hashem even over his snuff.

title.en: The king who must lift up the queen

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the holiness of Zos Chanukah comes down to the very lowest place, and brings the passuk 'she has fallen and will no longer rise' as the Gemara in Berachos and the Zohar read it: a king twice sent away the queen and called her back, and the third time she refused to return unless the king himself lifts her up. Every Chanukah reveals the light of Moshiach, and he says one must daven to be lifted and let oneself be lifted. He closes with a tefilah that the light of Moshiach revealed on Chanukah be fulfilled and Moshiach come.

oneLiner.en: At a Zos Chanukah gathering the Mashgiach gives his chaburah practical advice on learning, davening, Chofetz Chaim and Shabbos, and explains the Chanukah lights as the chinuch of the light of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by thanking Hashem and, with Yosef's words to his brothers and the Ba'al Shem Tov, says that wherever a person is sent he has something to repair. Then he offers advice. He asks the chaburah to learn at night where they daven. He describes tefillah rising through the worlds to Shemoneh Esrei and the descent of the bounty afterwards, comparing one who leaves early to a shopper who pays and leaves his bag on the counter. Following the Imrei Emes's letter, he urges learning two halachos of Chofetz Chaim daily with a chavrusa, and suggests Shabbos gatherings and using shalosh seudos. On Chanukah he brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the lights are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, and reads the nations' outcry against Jewish ownership of Eretz Yisroel through Rashi's first comment as a reason for joy. He closes with blessings for unity.

en: Where a person is sent is a sign from Hashem that he has something to repair there and a shlichus to fulfill.
The Mashgiach asks that the chaburah learn in the same beis medrash where they daven, with a fixed place for both tefillah and Torah.
The bounty gathered in Shemoneh Esrei descends in the parts of davening after it, so one should daven the whole davening and not leave early.
The Mashgiach proposes that each person learn two halachos of Chofetz Chaim daily with his chavrusa, finishing the sefer in a year.
The Chanukah lights lit generation after generation are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, which will then be revealed in full.

title.en: Tefillah rising through the worlds

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how davening rises from world to world, from pesukei dezimra to Shemoneh Esrei, where one stands before the King and asks for parnassah, refuos and everything. He tells of a man who davened there that a household helper not leave, and answers that one davens according to the plain meaning: to whom else should he ask?

title.en: The descent of the bounty after Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the bounty gathered in tefillah descends at Tachanun, Uva Letziyon and Aleinu, and compares one who leaves before then to a shopper who pays and leaves his bag on the counter. He rejects the claim that this is unnecessary, says it is not his own stringency but comes from great tzaddikim, and asks that people daven the whole davening.

title.en: The Imrei Emes and the sefer Chofetz Chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the chaburah once all learned the same sefer so they could discuss it, and now urges learning Chofetz Chaim. He tells how the Imrei Emes wrote a letter to his chassidim to learn it, saying he felt its benefit himself, and thereby broke the divide between chassidim and Litvaks; the Mashgiach adds that learning it made him a different person.

title.en: Two halachos a day with a chavrusa

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that holding back a forbidden word at every moment is constant yiras shamayim and conquest of the yetzer, a great nachas ruach to Hashem. He proposes two halachos a day with one's chavrusa, at the start or end of learning, and suggests Rabbi Shimon Finkelman's English book for learning at home with the family.

title.en: Shabbos gatherings and shalosh seudos

summary.en: After asking for a refuah shleimah, the Mashgiach speaks of feeling a sweetness in Shabbos. He remembers Friday nights as a young man, when ten or fifteen Jews sat together telling stories of tzaddikim and singing zemiros, the high point of his week, and urges coming together and using the hour of shalosh seudos, which makes a person better.

title.en: Chanukah lights and the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah lights are the light of Moshiach, and that the lights Jews kindle generation after generation gather until it is revealed in full; the Bnei Yissaschar calls them its chinuch. He then reads the nations' outcry that the Jews are robbers in Eretz Yisroel through Rashi's first comment on Bereishis, and says it is a reason to rejoice.

title.en: Blessings for unity and the third Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the gathering that, with the power of Chanukah, the honor of Heaven be revealed and the third Beis HaMikdash be built, with yeshuos, refuos and simcha. He stresses that love and friendship among Jews bring blessing, cites Rabbi Akiva's great principle and the tefillah of Rebbe Elimelech to see the good in one's fellow, and ends with l'chaim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that after Pesach, the Yom Tov of emunah, the Torah warns against the two things that damage emunah most, forbidden food and breaches of kedushah, and describes how the Satan in our generation floods the world with both.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling that Pesach is the Yom Tov of emunah and that matzah, which the Zohar calls the food of emunah, makes emunah part of a Jew's body. The two sedras read right after Pesach, Shemini on forbidden foods and Acharei on arayos, deal with the two greatest damagers of emunah. Treif food clogs the heart, as the Gemara reads 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem', and takes away a person's taste in Yiddishkeit and Shabbos. In the days before Moshiach the Satan, fighting for his life, floods the market with treif and doubtful hechsherim. The Mashgiach tells of the Skverer Rebbe's extreme care, the Rambam's answer to doubters of techiyas hameisim, and a tzaddik who found a kernel of wheat in his Pesach soup because he had not davened. He then turns to kedushas habris, describes the streets and media of today, and urges escaping the city, guarding the home, and keeping good company.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of emunah, and by eating matzah, the food of emunah, a Jew internalizes emunah into his very body.
The sedras after Pesach, Shemini and Acharei, address forbidden food and arayos because these two damage emunah more than anything else.
Forbidden food clogs the heart, so that a person loses his feeling and taste in Yiddishkeit and in Shabbos.
In the days before Moshiach the Satan, fighting for his life, floods the market with treif and unreliable hechsherim.
Care in kashrus is not enough on its own; a person must also daven to Hashem not to stumble.
The Satan of this generation has concentrated on breaching kedushah through the streets and the media, a test no earlier generation faced.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that Pesach is the Yom Tov of emunah and that eating matzah makes emunah part of a Jew's body. He then notes that the sedras after Pesach, Shemini and Acharei, deal with forbidden food and arayos, the two greatest damagers of emunah.

title.en: Treif food dulls the taste of Yiddishkeit

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Jews who taste the sweetness of Shabbos with bochurim who complain they feel nothing on Shabbos, and says they probably ate treif. He brings the Gemara that reads 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem': forbidden food clogs the heart.

title.en: The Satan floods the market with treif

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the days before Moshiach the Satan, sensing danger, fights with extra strength and floods the market with forbidden food. Before World War I no Jew ate treif; today ingredients are so complex and hechsherim so unreliable that hardly anyone can say he never ate treif.

title.en: The Skverer Rebbe and the Rambam's letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Skverer Rebbe refused freshly squeezed orange juice because his father never drank it, and baked his bread all year from wheat he had cut himself. He then brings the Rambam's letter answering people who doubted techiyas hameisim: they ask because they ate forbidden food.

title.en: Care and tefillah: the kernel in the soup

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges care in kashrus together with tefillah not to stumble, and tells of a tzaddik who cleaned for a month yet found a kernel of wheat in his soup at the Seder. Through a dream question he learned it happened because he had not davened for a kosher Pesach, and how a bird dropped it down the chimney.

title.en: Kedushas habris and the streets of today

summary.en: Turning to the second damager, the Mashgiach links Pesach and bris milah to Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and explains that bris milah is a lifelong mitzvah of guarding kedushah. He describes how today's streets, laws and media have made this test greater than in any generation, bringing the Medrash on 'goy naval' in Haazinu.

title.en: Practical guarding: city, home and friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up that emunah is ruined by forbidden food and breaches of kedushas habris, and urges whoever can to leave the city in summer and to keep radio, television and inciting literature out of the home. He stresses the influence of friends and brings the Rambam that one must move away from a bad neighborhood.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, seals the judgment of Yom Kippur and corresponds to Moshiach, and that it is a time to hope for the redemption and to daven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that on Zos Chanukah, the last day of Chanukah, a simple Jew can achieve through prayer what a tzaddik achieves on Rosh Hashanah. It is accepted that this is the time of gmar chasima tova, when the sealing of Yom Kippur ends, and the eighth light corresponds to Moshiach. There is an obligation to await Moshiach at every moment; at the judgment one is asked whether he hoped for the redemption, and 'for Your salvation we hope all day', said three times daily, gives the answer. The Rambam speaks of awaiting, not only believing. He then reads the Yalkut about the year Moshiach is revealed, when the kings of the nations provoke one another and Israel is told not to fear. He concludes that Jews must daven, since prayer can annul decrees, and asks everyone to say l'chaim with gmar chasima tova.

en: What a tzaddik can achieve through prayer on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah.
It is accepted among Jews that Zos Chanukah is the time of gmar chasima tova, when the sealing of Yom Kippur comes to its end.
Zos Chanukah, the eighth light, corresponds to Moshiach, so it is a time especially suited to hoping for him.
There is an obligation to await Moshiach at every moment, and one is asked at the judgment whether he hoped for the redemption.
The Yalkut describes the year Moshiach is revealed as a time when the kings of the nations provoke one another, and Israel is told not to fear.
Jews must daven, since prayer can annul decrees, even harsh ones.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos is Hashem's personal gift to Klal Yisroel, and that a Jew must prepare for it all week, through tefillah, kedushas habris, guarded speech, learning its halachos and honoring its food, in order to feel it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Hashem called Shabbos a good gift from His treasury and told Moshe to make it known, and explains with the parable of a chasan's flawless diamond that Shabbos is a personal sign between Hashem and Klal Yisroel. He then shows that the whole week revolves around Shabbos: every mitzvah and tefillah prepares for it, a Jew should long for it, and its fire must be kindled during the week. He teaches that Shabbos is reached through kedushas habris, that erev Shabbos is the day of Yosef and yesod, and that people who do not feel Shabbos did not prepare for it. He describes how the whole Shabbos davening, the seudos and the fish must feel like Shabbos, that Shabbos is a name of Hashem and is emunah, and that it must be guarded in speech. He closes with learning hilchos Shabbos and the holiness of Shabbos food.

en: Shabbos differs from every other mitzvah: it is a personal gift and a sign of the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and a Jew must know its worth.
All the mitzvos and tefillos of the week revolve around Shabbos and are a preparation for it.
Kedushas habris, guarding the mind and the eyes, is what brings a Jew to feel the holiness of Shabbos.
Those who do not feel Shabbos have not prepared for it during the week with kedushah and Torah.
Shabbos must be guarded in speech, because Hashem's work in creation was through speech.
The food of Shabbos carries great holiness, the holiness of the mann, and must be eaten in honor of Shabbos.

title.en: Shabbos, the gift from Hashem's treasury

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Hashem told Moshe He has a good gift in His treasury called Shabbos and that he should make it known, and asks why only Shabbos needed this. He answers with the parable of a chasan who sends his kallah a flawless diamond and must tell her it is not glass: Shabbos is a personal sign between Hashem and Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The whole week revolves around Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every mitzvah and tefillah of the week prepares for Shabbos and that a Jew should long for it like a chasan and kallah await the chuppah. He tells of chassidim leaving a melave malka at dawn who were greeted with the news that in six days it will be Shabbos again, recalls the European question whether a Jew 'has for Shabbos', and reads 'lo s'vaaru esh' as a call to kindle the fire of Shabbos during the week.

title.en: Praying for Shabbos; kedushas habris

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew should pray constantly to merit a bright Shabbos and its oneg, and mentions R' Aharon of Karlin's song of longing for Shabbos. He teaches that the holiness of Shabbos is reached through kedushas habris, guarding the mind and the eyes in a world sunk in impurity, and that a warm Shabbos is a sign that one withstood such a test.

title.en: Erev Shabbos is the day of Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the six weekdays correspond to six sefiros and that erev Shabbos is Yosef, middas hayesod, through which one prepares for Shabbos. He brings Chazal that Yosef kept Shabbos in Mitzrayim, describes the 'bechinah of Yosef' as a Jew careful about what he eats, and says that one sunk in kelipos cannot feel Shabbos, as people complain to him.

title.en: Preparation and the Shabbos tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one does not feel Shabbos because one did not prepare all week with kedushah and Torah. He brings the Panim Yafos that the whole Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei, not only its middle berachah, and the whole davening must feel like Shabbos, a tzaddik's teaching that at Nishmas one davens with the soul alone, and that teshuvah, from which the name Shabbos comes, brings a Jew close to Shabbos.

title.en: The Shabbos seudos; Shabbos as Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one eats all week to have strength to learn and daven and so to taste the Shabbos seudos, and tells of an old chassid who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos in the challah and in the fish. He brings the Zohar that Shabbos is a name of Hashem, so ehrliche Yidden avoid saying the word in an unclean place, explains that Shabbos is emunah, and urges davening to guard Shabbos.

title.en: Guarding Shabbos in speech; the Shabbos home

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from the passuk that Hashem rested on the seventh day that His work in creation was speech, so a Jew must guard Shabbos by measuring his words and not talking business at the seudos, but Torah, stories of tzaddikim and a word on the sedra. He describes the Shabbos home, kavod habayis, and the Shabbos lights as honor and shalom bayis.

title.en: Hilchos Shabbos and the holiness of Shabbos food

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges learning hilchos Shabbos, at least from kitzurim, and seforim on the greatness of Shabbos such as the Sidduro shel Shabbos. He describes how ehrliche Yidden have in mind the holiness of Shabbos in every spoonful, tells of R' Dovid Biderman eating a spoiled cholent rather than shame Shabbos food, says the food of Shabbos holds the holiness of the mann, and closes with a gut Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the three ascending stages of Shabbos, culminating in Shabbos mincha and shalosh seudos, a time of yichud beyond place and time, and says one must want and pray to truly feel Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the three parts of Shabbos: Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, which parallel the three parts of the Beis Hamikdash and the stages of kiddushin, nisuin and yichud. Each part has its tefillah and its seudah, and the Avos come as guests to our seudos, so the table should be run to please them. Mincha is the highest point: its Amidah has no pesukim, its seudah is simple, and it is a 'nachalah without boundaries'. Through a question of the Avnei Nezer about the manna kept in the Kodesh Hakodashim, he shows that what is beyond place is beyond time, and so is shalosh seudos. The time itself is a mikveh, Moshe Rabbeinu passed away then, and the Ba'al Shem Tov had it eaten together. He ends with the mashal of the weary traveler, the story of R' Shlomo of Karlin's sock, and the call to want to feel Shabbos.

en: Shabbos has three stages, Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, like the courtyard, the Heichal and the Kodesh Hakodashim, and like kiddushin, nisuin and yichud.
The Avos come as guests to the three seudos, so the seudah should be conducted to please the guests, with divrei Torah, joy and warmth.
Shabbos mincha and shalosh seudos are beyond place and time, the yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like the Kodesh Hakodashim.
The higher the kedushah of Shabbos, the less it is felt, so Friday night is felt most and mincha least.
One must want to feel Shabbos and ask Hashem for it; keeping Shabbos without trying to feel it leaves a person like a wooden bench in Gan Eden.
